How We Refute Claims: Automatic Fact-Checking through Flaw
Identification and Explanation
Wei-Yu Kao
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
An-Zi Yen
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
Hsinchu, Taiwan
wayner.cs09@nycu.edu.tw
Hsinchu, Taiwan
azyen@nycu.edu.tw
ABSTRACT
a claim false. For instance, in the question answering approach, the
generated questions predominantly focus on straightforward facts
such as who, when, where, and how. In real-world scenarios, decep-
tive claims are often intricately crafted to mislead without falling
into obvious pitfalls, strategically distorting a minor segment of the
claim. This is precisely why professional fact-checkers thoughtfully
analyze claims from diverse perspectives, assessing not only the
literal accuracy of the statement but also considering elements such
as tone, context, and its consistency with established facts. Thus, it
becomes imperative to identify the specific flaws within a claim to
comprehensively confirm and elucidate its veracity in an automatic
fact-checking process.
Automated fact-checking is a crucial task in the governance of in-
ternet content. Although various studies utilize advanced models
to tackle this issue, a significant gap persists in addressing complex
real-world rumors and deceptive claims. To address this challenge,
this paper explores the novel task of flaw-oriented fact-checking, in-
cluding aspect generation and flaw identification. We also introduce
RefuteClaim, a new framework designed specifically for this task.
Given the absence of an existing dataset, we present FlawCheck, a
dataset created by extracting and transforming insights from expert
reviews into relevant aspects and identified flaws. The experimen-
tal results underscore the efficacy of RefuteClaim, particularly in
classifying and elucidating false claims.
CCS CONCEPTS
• Computing methodologies →Natural language processing;
• Information systems →Web applications.
KEYWORDS
Claim Refutation, Flaw Identification, Explainable Fact-Checking
1
INTRODUCTION
As the World Wide Web continues to expand, an overwhelming
amount of information is flooding the internet. With limited time
available, individuals often struggle to comprehensively grasp con-
tent and may be adversely influenced by problematic claims. Ac-
curately assessing the veracity of a claim demands considerable
time and effort from fact-checking organizations and experts, who
meticulously gather relevant evidence and scrutinize the facts and
assumptions. Hence, in the quest to efficiently identify a plethora
of false statements on the internet, numerous studies have investi-
gated automatic fact-checking.
arXiv:2401.15312v1  [cs.CL]  27 Jan 2024
To address the challenge at hand, we first employ aspect genera-
tion to determine the most crucial aspects associated with the claim,
around which evaluation should be focused. Based on evidence, our
model synthesizes explanations for these distinct aspects. Then, we
carefully select seven critical flaws from an initial set of twenty-two
false labels used by various fact-checking organizations to debunk
claims. These flaws are grouped into three distinct categories, each
influencing the outcome of the fact-checking process in unique
ways. The first category includes three explicit flaws that can be
identified by evaluating the claim’s compatibility with the evidence:
contradicting facts, exaggeration, and understatement. In the
second category, we introduce two more nuanced flaws: occasional
faltering and insufficient support. Fact-checkers working within
this realm must employ critical reasoning to envisage potential
scenarios where the claim may not hold true. A claim may seem
convincing initially but fail to maintain its validity or soundness
over time and across different scenarios. The final category encapsu-
lates the two most complex flaws: problematic assumptions and
existence of alternative explanations. Identifying these particu-
lar flaws is a more intricate process, as it requires fact-checkers to
consider a wider context and often demands extensive background
knowledge that may not be demonstrated in the evidence at hand.
Details will be elaborated in the following section.
In the absence of an existing dataset, we extend WatClaim-
Check [7], utilizing a large language model (LLM) to infer the
aspects and flaws of claims based on review articles, thereby con-
structing the FlawCheck dataset.1 Subsequently, we present Refute-
Claim, a novel framework designed to guide the review process
in creating comprehensive fact-checking articles to emulate the
quality and depth of articles generated by human experts.
In summary, our contributions are summarized as follows:
Research on automatic fact-checking can be broadly categorized
into veracity classification and justification generation, with a pre-
dominant focus on the former. Although veracity classification is
essential for prompt assessment of claims, justification generation
plays a more pivotal role in producing explainable results and fa-
cilitating comprehensive fact-checking. To generate justifications
in natural language, early studies [1, 10] proposed directly extract-
ing sentences from reliable sources such as news content. More
recent work [2, 8, 9] explores the approach of question answering,
which involves generating questions related to specific facts within
the claims. By answering these generated questions using support-
ing evidence, models predict and articulate the authenticity of the
claims, fostering more robust fact-checking.
• We introduce a novel flaw-checking task that entails the
examination of the seven flaws, reflecting the complexities
of real-world automatic fact-checking scenarios.

Conference acronym ’XX, June 03–05, 2018, Woodstock, NY
Wei-Yu Kao and An-Zi Yen
• We present the FlawCheck dataset, which encompasses dis-
tinct aspects and explanations for the seven flaws associated
with each claim. This dataset encapsulates the expertise of
human fact-checking professionals.
• We propose RefuteClaim, a framework that integrates as-
pect generation and flaw identification into an automatic
fact-checking pipeline. Experimental results show promising
performance, both in classifying and elucidating false claims.
2
FLAW-ORIENTED FACT-CHECKING
In this study, we develop RefuteClaim, which incorporates aspect
generation along with flaw identification and explanation for fact-
checking. The definitions are provided as follows.
2.1
Aspect Generation
Occasional faltering: A claim falters at times when it is presented
as universally true, but cannot be consistently sustained. For exam-
ple, the claim that “electric cars are always better for the environ-
ment” may falter in regions where electricity is primarily generated
from coal, potentially making the environmental benefits less clear-
cut. This inconsistency reveals that the claim does not account for
specific conditions where it may not hold true.
Insufficient support: Claims should be backed up by evidence.
Support is insufficient when assertions are made without the nec-
essary substantiation. For instance, claiming that “a particular diet
causes weight loss in all individuals” without citing scientific studies
or statistical data is an unsupported statement.
Problematic assumptions: This type of flaw arises when a claim
is based on assumptions that are not validated or are questionable.
Problematic assumptions can lead to incorrect conclusions. An
example would be assuming that “increased internet usage directly
causes poor social skills,” which ignores potential factors like the
type of internet usage or individual differences.
Existence of alternative explanations: Even if a claim seems
plausible, other explanations may account for the observed facts.
A flaw exists when a claim does not consider or rule out such
alternative explanations. For example, the conclusion that “rising
smartphone sales are due solely to improved technology” ignores
other possible factors such as marketing strategies or changes in
consumer behavior.
Note that a single claim may incorporate several distinct flaws,
and the composition of aspects is indeed diverse.
3
DATASET CONSTRUCTION
Aspect generation aids in identifying and focusing on the key ele-
ments around which the evaluation of a claim revolves. The goal
is to determine the most crucial aspects associated with a claim
to guide subsequent flaw identification and explanation. Aspects
represent the specific dimensions or attributes that are integral to
evaluating the validity of a claim, for example, a statement asserting
that a particular politician engaged in corrupt practices during an
election campaign. In this context, aspects could include:
Legal investigations: Evaluating whether there are ongoing or
concluded legal investigations into the alleged corrupt practices.
Financial transactions: Scrutinizing financial transactions related
to the campaign to identify any irregular activities.
Political motivations: Investigating if there are political motiva-
tions behind the accusations, such as rivalry strategies.
Legal precedents: Examining similar cases in the past to under-
stand how they were adjudicated.
The relevant evidence associated with a claim may lead to various
aspects. In this work, our model explains up to four distinct aspects.
Due to the demand for premise articles and complete review articles
written by human experts, we selected WatClaimCheck [7] as our
data source, given its ample and varied collection from eight fact-
checking websites. In this study, we extend 33,721 claims and their
metadata in WatClaimCheck to facilitate the proposed flaw-oriented
fact-checking task, leading to the creation of FlawCheck.
2.2
Flaw Identification and Explanation
Since the original content in WatClaimCheck includes a signifi-
cant amount of irrelevant web crawl data, we collected the web data
again and cleaned it to ensure relatively clean review articles for the
evaluation of justification generation. Then, we harness the capabil-
ities of GPT-3.5-turbo to distill expert opinions from review arti-
cles and transform them into the various aspects and identify flaws.
Given an input claim𝐶𝑖and a review article 𝑅𝑖, we initially generate
four silver ground-truth aspects A𝑖= {𝐴𝑖,1,𝐴𝑖,2, . . . ,𝐴𝑖,𝑛}, where
1 ≤𝑛≤4. The aspects may represent coarse-grained facts refer-
enced by the claim. Following the same process, taking 𝐶𝑖and 𝑅𝑖,
we utilize GPT-3.5-turbo to transform the human expert argumen-
tation to elaborate the presence of flaws F𝑖= {𝐹𝑖,1, 𝐹𝑖,2, . . . , 𝐹𝑖,7}.
Furthermore, to facilitate the evaluation of veracity classification,
we reassigned the labels in WatClaimCheck due to inaccuracies in
their arrangement, for instance, classifying the label “Pants on Fire”
to “Partially True/False.” We define four labels—Incorrect, Partly
false, Unproven, and Correct—based on the original ratings obtained
from each fact-checking website. FlawCheck’s label distribution in
the training and testing sets is as follows: “True” with 5,272 and
657, “Unproven” with 805 and 112, “Partly false” with 3,429 and
451, and “False” with 17,470 and 2,153 instances, respectively. This
The process of flaw identification and explanation involves examin-
ing statements or claims critically to identify inaccuracies or logical
inconsistencies. Here we define and detail seven types of flaws that
may be present in a claim:
Contradicting facts: When a claim is presented, it must align
with established facts. A contradicting fact occurs when the claim
directly opposes known and verified information. For instance, the
claim that “the Earth is flat” contradicts the overwhelming scientific
evidence that the Earth is an oblate spheroid. It is crucial to cross-
reference claims with reliable data sources to detect such flaws.
Exaggeration: Exaggeration is a flaw where the truth is stretched
beyond its actual proportions. This can be done to make something
appear more significant or severe than it really is. For example, stat-
ing that “everyone hates the new policy” is likely an exaggeration,
as it is improbable that every single person has a negative view.
Understatement: An understatement minimizes the significance
of something in a way that misrepresents the truth and downplays
important facts. Saying “climate change is a minor issue” is an
understatement because it fails to convey the widespread consensus
on the seriousness of climate change impacts.

This paper explores the process of forming a flaw-checking perspec-
tive to generate justifications in an effort to emulate the quality of
fact-checking conducted by human professionals. We introduce the
novel task of flaw-oriented fact-checking and present FlawCheck, a
dataset encompassing the critical aspects identified by experts and
seven pivotal flaws that demand evaluation. A pilot framework, Re-
futeClaim, is proposed. The experimental results highlight the effec-
tiveness of RefuteClaim in elucidating and classifying false claims.
As a pioneering work in studying flaw-oriented fact-checking, fur-
ther investigation is required to explore the optimal utilization of
aspects and flaws.
